description: I’m Gourab, an astronomy PhD candidate at Mizzou with experience in Python and JWST image analysis. I’m forming a team to build a public web tool that lets anyone flip between SPHEREx images of the same patch of sky to spot objects that move. I’d love to work with teammates interested in web development, data visualization, Python, or science storytelling. You don’t need an astronomy background to join!
summary: Sky in Motion is a web tool that lets anyone enter a sky position and watch NASA SPHEREx infrared images of it change over time. It finds every SPHEREx exposure of that position, cleans and aligns them, and combines them into one frame per survey visit. Users can blink the frames, subtract one visit from another so that only moving or varying objects remain, overlay Gaia star positions, and see a quick-look spectrum. It addresses the challenge by turning SPHEREx’s complex spectral images into a simple “spot what moved” view for the public.
details: Sky in Motion takes a sky position or object name and returns a short “movie” of that patch of sky from NASA’s SPHEREx mission. A Python backend (FastAPI, Astropy, reproject) searches the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive for every SPHEREx exposure covering the position, downloads small cutouts, subtracts the zodiacal light model, masks bad pixels, and reprojects each exposure onto a common north-up grid. Because SPHEREx wavelength varies across each detector, exposures are median-combined per detector band and per survey visit. A browser viewer (plain JavaScript) blinks the visits, subtracts any two so that only moving or varying objects remain, co-adds all visits, overlays Gaia DR3 positions moved to each frame’s date, and plots a quick-look spectrum and brightness over time. Coordinates in the URL make every view shareable. Tested on all five challenge targets using 966 real exposures; the difference image of Barnard’s Star shows its northward motion between August 2025 and August 2026. Limits: very bright stars saturate, the spectrum is uncalibrated, and the fainter targets have not yet been assessed. WISE 0855-0714 is not detected in a co-add of 45 band-D6 exposures, and R Draconis saturates the detector in band D3; the tool reports both through its flags and measurements.
